svg.title: Kizuna architecture: the Rust kernel on the device and the SQL pack in your Supabase project, with no Kizuna service between them.
svg.desc: A Kizuna deployment has two halves, and nothing of Kizuna's runs between them. On the device, your app (React, Vue, Expo, Swift, or Kotlin) calls the app client, createKizunaSync or KizunaSyncClient, which reaches the Rust kernel through one of three bridges: a WebAssembly worker, N-API, or UniFFI. The kernel card, kizunasync-engine, lists the outbox with three queued mutations, push and pull, the checkpoint, and the attachment queue, and the kernel owns the local SQLite store through rusqlite. Your Supabase project holds the kizunasync schema with its pull and push functions, _changelog, _tombstones, _verdicts, and the triggers on synced tables, next to your tables under RLS, Storage for attachment bytes, and Realtime on kizunasync:<table> topics. A thin divider between the halves carries the label no Kizuna service. In the loop, a chip carrying three mutations rides the push wire to the kizunasync schema, your tables flash as the rows are written under RLS, and an applied chip rides back while the outbox count drops from 3 to 0. A pull chip then brings a new checkpoint to the kernel, a bytes chip travels its own dashed wire from the kernel to Storage, and Realtime rings and sends a wake pulse to the kernel. The outbox shows three queued mutations again as the loop repeats.
svg.text: Two halves. Nothing of ours in between.
The kernel answers screens from local SQLite on the device; the SQL pack speaks the protocol in the Supabase project you own.
